Streaming data: A continuous, unbounded sequence of events generated in real-time from sources like IoT devices, sensors, or transactions. Unlike batch data, it has no fixed end and must be processed on the fly as it arrives.
Batch processing: Collecting data into a finite chunk (a file, a table, a query result) and processing it all at once, typically on a schedule. The job ends when the data is exhausted — the opposite of an open-ended stream.
Unbounded: Having no defined end. A streaming source is unbounded: the consumer keeps running and waits for the next event rather than finishing when the current data runs out.
Publish/subscribe: A messaging pattern where producers (publishers) send messages to a named destination and any number of consumers (subscribers) register interest and receive them. Producers and consumers are decoupled — neither needs to know about the other.
Broker: The server that receives messages from producers and delivers them to subscribed consumers. HiveMQ, EMQX, and RabbitMQ are brokers; Kafka brokers play the same role in a cluster.
Topic: A named channel on a broker that messages are published to and consumed from. Subscribers express interest in a topic to receive its messages.
Producer: A client that publishes messages to a broker (for example a sensor script, or PDI's MQTT Producer step).
Consumer: A client that subscribes to a stream and reads messages from it. In PDI the consumer steps are MQTT Consumer, Kafka Consumer, and AMQP Consumer.
Parent/child transformation: The PDI streaming pattern. The parent transformation holds the consumer step, which collects incoming messages into batches; each batch is handed to a child transformation that processes the records. The same pattern is used for every streaming protocol.
Get records from stream: The PDI step that surfaces a batch of streamed messages as rows. It produces rows, so it must be the first step in the child transformation; you cannot place it mid-stream.
Batch (streaming): A group of messages the consumer collects before invoking the child transformation. It is flushed when the first threshold is met — either a Duration (ms) time window or a Number of records count.
MQTT: Message Queuing Telemetry Transport — a lightweight publish/subscribe protocol designed for the Internet of Things. Minimal overhead makes it ideal for constrained devices and sensor networks.
QoS: Quality of Service in MQTT, controlling delivery guarantees: 0 (at most once, lowest latency, can lose messages), 1 (at least once, may duplicate), 2 (exactly once, highest overhead).
Clean session: An MQTT connection flag. When true the broker keeps no state for the client; when false the broker persists the client's subscriptions and queued QoS 1/2 messages between connections.
HiveMQ: An enterprise MQTT broker used in this course to carry industrial robot-sensor telemetry. Run as a Docker container exposing its TCP listener on port 1883 and a Control Center on 9090.
EMQX: A scalable open-source MQTT broker used in the logistics / predictive-maintenance workshop. Exposes an MQTT TCP listener on 1883 and a dashboard on 18083.
SCADA: Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition — software and hardware systems that gather and control data from industrial equipment. Most SCADA and MES systems support MQTT, making it the natural ingestion protocol for factory telemetry.
IoT: Internet of Things — networks of connected devices and sensors that publish data, often over lightweight protocols like MQTT because of their limited memory and power.
Apache Kafka: A distributed event-streaming platform for high-volume, fault-tolerant publish/subscribe pipelines. Built around a distributed commit log, it provides durability and high throughput for producers and consumers.
KRaft: Kafka Raft metadata mode — Kafka's controller architecture that removes the ZooKeeper dependency by managing cluster metadata within Kafka itself using the Raft consensus protocol, simplifying deployment.
Partition: A Kafka topic is split into partitions — ordered, append-only logs. Partitions allow a topic to scale across brokers and let consumers in a group divide the work.
Offset: A sequential ID that uniquely identifies a record within a Kafka partition. Consumers track offsets to know what they have read and where to resume.
Consumer group: A set of Kafka consumers that cooperate to read a topic. Each consumer in the group is assigned a subset of the topic's partitions, so the group shares the load.
auto.offset.reset: A Kafka consumer option that sets where to begin reading when no committed offset exists: earliest (from the start of the topic) or latest (only new messages).
Schema Registry: A centralized repository, separate from the brokers, that stores and validates the schemas describing topic messages, and handles serialization/deserialization. It uses Kafka as its durable backend.
AMQP: Advanced Message Queuing Protocol — a standardized, open broker protocol for reliable, decoupled messaging. Supports asynchronous communication, system decoupling, resilience, and load balancing.
RabbitMQ: A popular open-source message broker that implements AMQP. Used in this course to carry room-sensor data (temperature, pressure, humidity) and route it to queues by routing key.
Exchange: In AMQP, the entity a producer publishes to. The exchange routes messages to queues using bindings and routing keys, rather than the producer writing to a queue directly.
Binding: A link between an exchange and a queue that tells the exchange which messages to route to that queue.
Routing key: A message attribute the exchange inspects to decide how to route a message to queues. With DIRECT or TOPIC exchange types you specify one or more routing keys.
Fanout: The default RabbitMQ exchange type. It broadcasts every message it receives to all bound queues, ignoring routing keys.
Queue: In AMQP, the structure that stores messages until a consumer retrieves them. Queues can be durable (survive restarts), exclusive (one connection), or auto-delete (removed when the last consumer disconnects).
Durable: A broker object (queue or exchange) configured to be saved to disk so it survives a broker restart, as opposed to a transient object that is lost.
MQTT Producer: The PDI step that publishes a message field to an MQTT broker on a given topic, with configurable QoS and client ID.
Backpressure: Controls that prevent a fast stream from overwhelming the consumer — for example the message prefetch limit (how many messages PDI queues in memory) and the maximum concurrent batches.
